lesson.title: Mirror Images: Spotting Even Symmetry and Its All-Cosine Series
lesson.summary: A waveform has even symmetry when f(-t) equals f(t), a mirror image across the vertical axis, and that single geometric fact guarantees every sine term in its Fourier series is exactly zero.
lesson.body:
You already know one even function intimately: the cosine itself, since cos(-omega t) = cos(omega t) for any angle. A periodic waveform has even symmetry when the same mirror property holds for the whole waveform, not just one cycle of it: pick t = 0 as the vertical axis, and the left half of the graph is a perfect mirror image of the right half. Sinusoidal waveforms built purely from cosines are the simplest examples, but plenty of non-sinusoidal periodic waveforms are even too, as long as you choose where to place t = 0 correctly.

Even symmetry matters because of what it does to the Fourier series sine coefficients. Recall bn = (2/T) times the integral of f(t) sin(n omega0 t) over one period. Sine is an odd function, and if f(t) is even, the product f(t) sin(n omega0 t) is even times odd, which is odd. The integral of any odd function over a symmetric interval like -T/2 to T/2 is exactly zero, because the negative-time half exactly cancels the positive-time half. So for any even waveform, every single bn is zero automatically, without computing a single integral. The Fourier series collapses to f(t) = a0 + the sum of an cos(n omega0 t): a DC term plus cosines only, no sines anywhere.

Here is a fully worked example. Take a triangular wave defined over one period as f(t) = A(1 - 4|t|/T) for -T/2 less than or equal to t less than or equal to T/2, which rises to a peak of A at t = 0 and falls linearly to -A at each edge t = plus or minus T/2. Because the formula depends only on the absolute value of t, f(-t) = A(1 - 4|-t|/T) = A(1 - 4|t|/T) = f(t): even symmetry, confirmed directly from the formula. Carrying out the integrals confirms the prediction: a0 works out to exactly 0 (the waveform swings symmetrically between +A and -A, so its average is zero), and an works out to 8A / (pi squared n squared) for every odd n, and exactly 0 for every even n; every bn is 0, exactly as even symmetry requires. As a check, plug t = 0 into the series: f(0) should equal A, and indeed (8A / pi squared) times the sum of 1/n squared over odd n equals (8A / pi squared) times (pi squared / 8) = A, which matches. For a concrete instance, a 6 V peak, 1 kHz triangle wave has a1 = 8(6)/(pi squared) = 4.86 V at 1 kHz, a3 = 4.86/9 = 0.54 V at 3 kHz, and a5 = 4.86/25 = 0.19 V at 5 kHz, with zero sine content at every harmonic.

Notice, too, that the triangle wave's coefficients fall off as 1/n squared, much faster than the square wave's 1/n from the Harmonic Content chapter. That is a general and reliable pattern in Fourier analysis: a waveform with an abrupt jump, like the square wave, converges slowly; a waveform that is continuous but has a sharp corner, like this triangle wave, converges faster. Even symmetry itself, though, is a purely geometric test you can apply by eye before doing any integration, and it is the mirror image companion to the odd symmetry test covered next.
